#!/bin/bash

# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables in an unquoted
# assignment slot, then reference them only as "$VAR". Never interpolate
#  inside a quoted context - sanitize() (shlex.quote) wraps
# dangerous values in single quotes, which are literal (and command
# substitution stays active) inside a double-quoted or single-quoted slot.
KIND=deployments
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=boutique
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""

# Collapse multi-line jq expressions (LLMs sometimes write multi-line jq)
# Note: use $'\n' syntax instead of '\n' because Jinja2 interprets \n as literal newlines
JQ_FILTER='.items[] | {name: .metadata.name, res: [.spec.template.spec.containers[] | {n: .name, r: .resources, env: [.env[]? | {name, value}]}], annot: .metadata.annotations}'
JQ_FILTER=$(printf '%s' "$JQ_FILTER" | tr $'\n\r' '  ')

err_file=$(mktemp)
PROCESSED=0
NOTES='[]'
SCOPE='null'

add_note() {
  NOTES=$(jq -c --arg note "$1" '. + [$note]' <<< "$NOTES")
}

uri_encode() {
  jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'
}

fail() {
  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
  rm -f "$err_file"
  jq -n --arg stderr "$1 $err_content" --argjson total "$PROCESSED" --argjson notes "$NOTES" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    '{total_items_processed: $total, matches_found: 0, results: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  exit 0
}

# The namespace becomes part of the raw API path, so anything other than a valid
# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && ! [[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" =~ ^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$ ]]; then
  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."
fi

# Get the API path for the resource kind using kubectl
# Match the resource name (first column) as an EXACT string, not a
# grep regex - otherwise a kind like '.*' or 'a|b' would match the
# wrong resource.
CANDIDATES=$(kubectl api-resources --no-headers 2>>"$err_file" | awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind')
API_INFO=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | head -1)
# `kubectl api-resources` sorts by group name, so a CRD reusing a built-in
# plural (e.g. Calico's crd.projectcalico.org networkpolicies) can be listed
# before networking.k8s.io. Pick what `kubectl get` picks: the core group,
# then the first group in server discovery order (/apis).
if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -c .)" -gt 1 ] && [[ "$API_INFO" != *" v1 "* ]]; then

  for group in $API_GROUPS; do
    match=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -F " $group/" | head -1)
    if [ -n "$match" ]; then
      API_INFO="$match"
      break
    fi
  done
fi

if [ -z "$API_INFO" ]; then
  fail "Unable to find resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

if [[ "$API_INFO" == *" true "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=true
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ true .*//')
elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=false
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')
else
  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."
fi

# Trim trailing spaces from prefix and collapse internal spaces
PREFIX=$(echo "$PREFIX" | sed 's/  *$//' | sed 's/  */ /g')

IFS=' ' read -ra PREFIX_FIELDS <<< "$PREFIX"
FIELD_COUNT=0
for field in "${PREFIX_FIELDS[@]}"; do
  ((FIELD_COUNT++))
done

  API_VERSION="${PREFIX_FIELDS[$((FIELD_COUNT - 1))]}"
else
  API_VERSION=""
fi

  fail "Unable to parse API info for resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# cluster-scoped kinds ignore the namespace (as kubectl does)

  API_BASE="/api/v1"
else
  API_BASE="/apis/${API_VERSION}"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && [ "$NAMESPACED" = "true" ]; then
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/namespaces/${SEL_NAMESPACE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
else

    add_note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${RESOURCE_NAME} is cluster-scoped."
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
fi

# then reference them only as "$VAR" - never interpolate 
# inside a quoted context. See kubernetes_jq_query for the rationale.
KIND=nodes
CUSTOM_COLUMNS='NAME:.metadata.name,CPU:.status.allocatable.cpu,MEM:.status.allocatable.memory,READY:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status'
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=
FILTER_PATTERN=
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""
[ "$FILTER_PATTERN" = "None" ] && FILTER_PATTERN=""

# kubectl ignores -n for cluster-scoped kinds; say so instead of reporting a namespace that wasn't applied
NOTES='[]'
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
  is_kind() { awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind || index($1, kind ".") == 1 {found = 1} END {exit !found}'; }
  if kubectl api-resources --namespaced=false -o name 2>/dev/null | is_kind \
    && ! kubectl api-resources --namespaced=true -o name 2>/dev/null | is_kind; then
    NOTES=$(jq -nc --arg note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${KIND} is cluster-scoped." '[$note]')
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
fi

SCOPE_ARGS=()
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(-n "$SEL_NAMESPACE")
else
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(--all-namespaces)
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(-l "$SEL_LABELS")
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SCOPE_ARGS+=(--field-selector "$SEL_FIELDS")
fi

err_file=$(mktemp)
output=$(kubectl get "$KIND" "${SCOPE_ARGS[@]}" -o custom-columns="$CUSTOM_COLUMNS" 2>"$err_file")
kubectl_exit=$?
err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

SCOPE='null'
if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
  SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
    '{namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
      label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
      field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')
fi

if [ $kubectl_exit -ne 0 ] || [ -z "$output" ]; then
  if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
    jq -n --arg stderr "$err_content" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
      '{count: 0, header: null, rows: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  else
    echo "=== STDERR ==="
    echo "$err_content"
    echo "=== ROWS ==="
    echo "=== COUNT ==="
    echo 0
  fi
  exit 0
fi

# Split header and data rows
header=$(echo "$output" | head -1)
if [ -n "$FILTER_PATTERN" ]; then
  data=$(echo "$output" | tail -n +2 | grep -E -- "$FILTER_PATTERN" || true)
else
  data=$(echo "$output" | tail -n +2)
fi

if command -v jq &>/dev/null; then
  if [ -n "$data" ]; then
    count=$(echo "$data" | wc -l)
  else
    count=0
  fi
  # Rows go through stdin, not --argjson, so large tables don't hit "Argument list too long"
  printf '%s' "$data" | jq -R . | jq -s \
    --argjson count "$count" \
    --arg header "$header" \
    --arg stderr "$err_content" \
    --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
    '{count: $count, header: $header, rows: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
else
  echo "=== STDERR ==="
  echo "$err_content"
  echo "=== HEADER ==="
  echo "$header"
  echo "=== ROWS ==="
  echo "$data"
  echo "=== COUNT ==="
  if [ -n "$data" ]; then echo "$data" | wc -l; else echo 0; fi
fi

#!/bin/bash

# SECURITY: assign sanitized params to shell variables in an unquoted
# assignment slot, then reference them only as "$VAR". Never interpolate
#  inside a quoted context - sanitize() (shlex.quote) wraps
# dangerous values in single quotes, which are literal (and command
# substitution stays active) inside a double-quoted or single-quoted slot.
KIND=pods
# 'namespace' is also a Jinja global (namespace()), so it is defined even when omitted
SEL_NAMESPACE=
SEL_LABELS=
SEL_FIELDS=null
# Strict tool calls send null for unset optional params, which renders as 'None'
[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" = "None" ] && SEL_NAMESPACE=""
[ "$SEL_LABELS" = "None" ] && SEL_LABELS=""
[ "$SEL_FIELDS" = "None" ] && SEL_FIELDS=""

# Collapse multi-line jq expressions (LLMs sometimes write multi-line jq)
# Note: use $'\n' syntax instead of '\n' because Jinja2 interprets \n as literal newlines
JQ_FILTER='.items[] | select(.metadata.namespace != "boutique") | {ns: .metadata.namespace, name: .metadata.name, node: .spec.nodeName, cpu_req: [.spec.containers[]?.resources.requests.cpu], cpu_lim: [.spec.containers[]?.resources.limits.cpu], phase: .status.phase}'
JQ_FILTER=$(printf '%s' "$JQ_FILTER" | tr $'\n\r' '  ')

err_file=$(mktemp)
PROCESSED=0
NOTES='[]'
SCOPE='null'

add_note() {
  NOTES=$(jq -c --arg note "$1" '. + [$note]' <<< "$NOTES")
}

uri_encode() {
  jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'
}

fail() {
  err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
  rm -f "$err_file"
  jq -n --arg stderr "$1 $err_content" --argjson total "$PROCESSED" --argjson notes "$NOTES" --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
    '{total_items_processed: $total, matches_found: 0, results: [], stderr: $stderr, scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'
  exit 0
}

# The namespace becomes part of the raw API path, so anything other than a valid
# namespace name (e.g. 'default/services/x:80/proxy/?') could reach other API endpoints
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && ! [[ "$SEL_NAMESPACE" =~ ^[a-z0-9]([-a-z0-9]{0,61}[a-z0-9])?$ ]]; then
  fail "Invalid namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}': must be a Kubernetes namespace name (lowercase letters, digits and '-')."
fi

# Get the API path for the resource kind using kubectl
# Match the resource name (first column) as an EXACT string, not a
# grep regex - otherwise a kind like '.*' or 'a|b' would match the
# wrong resource.
CANDIDATES=$(kubectl api-resources --no-headers 2>>"$err_file" | awk -v kind="$KIND" '$1 == kind')
API_INFO=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | head -1)
# `kubectl api-resources` sorts by group name, so a CRD reusing a built-in
# plural (e.g. Calico's crd.projectcalico.org networkpolicies) can be listed
# before networking.k8s.io. Pick what `kubectl get` picks: the core group,
# then the first group in server discovery order (/apis).
if [ "$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -c .)" -gt 1 ] && [[ "$API_INFO" != *" v1 "* ]]; then
  API_GROUPS=$(kubectl get --raw /apis 2>/dev/null | jq -r '.groups[].name' 2>/dev/null)
  if [ -z "$API_GROUPS" ]; then
    add_note "Several API groups serve '${KIND}' and server discovery (/apis) failed, so the first group listed by kubectl api-resources was used."
  fi
  for group in $API_GROUPS; do
    match=$(printf '%s\n' "$CANDIDATES" | grep -F " $group/" | head -1)
    if [ -n "$match" ]; then
      API_INFO="$match"
      break
    fi
  done
fi

if [ -z "$API_INFO" ]; then
  fail "Unable to find resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Extract NAMESPACED value
if [[ "$API_INFO" == *" true "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=true
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ true .*//')
elif [[ "$API_INFO" == *" false "* ]]; then
  NAMESPACED=false
  PREFIX=$(echo "$API_INFO" | sed 's/ false .*//')
else
  fail "Could not parse API info for '${KIND}'."
fi

# Trim trailing spaces from prefix and collapse internal spaces
PREFIX=$(echo "$PREFIX" | sed 's/  *$//' | sed 's/  */ /g')

IFS=' ' read -ra PREFIX_FIELDS <<< "$PREFIX"
FIELD_COUNT=0
for field in "${PREFIX_FIELDS[@]}"; do
  ((FIELD_COUNT++))
done

RESOURCE_NAME="${PREFIX_FIELDS[0]}"
if [ $FIELD_COUNT -ge 2 ]; then
  API_VERSION="${PREFIX_FIELDS[$((FIELD_COUNT - 1))]}"
else
  API_VERSION=""
fi

if [ -z "$API_VERSION" ] || [ -z "$RESOURCE_NAME" ]; then
  fail "Unable to parse API info for resource kind '${KIND}'."
fi

# Build API path: namespaced kinds can be listed within one namespace;
# cluster-scoped kinds ignore the namespace (as kubectl does)
if [[ "$API_VERSION" == "v1" ]]; then
  API_BASE="/api/v1"
else
  API_BASE="/apis/${API_VERSION}"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ] && [ "$NAMESPACED" = "true" ]; then
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/namespaces/${SEL_NAMESPACE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
else
  if [ -n "$SEL_NAMESPACE" ]; then
    add_note "namespace '${SEL_NAMESPACE}' ignored: ${RESOURCE_NAME} is cluster-scoped."
    SEL_NAMESPACE=""
  fi
  API_PATH="${API_BASE}/${RESOURCE_NAME}"
fi

SELECTOR_QUERY=""
if [ -n "$SEL_LABELS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&labelSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_LABELS")"
fi
if [ -n "$SEL_FIELDS" ]; then
  SELECTOR_QUERY="${SELECTOR_QUERY}&fieldSelector=$(uri_encode "$SEL_FIELDS")"
fi

SCOPE=$(jq -nc --arg resource "$RESOURCE_NAME" --arg api_version "$API_VERSION" \
  --arg namespace "$SEL_NAMESPACE" --arg labels "$SEL_LABELS" --arg fields "$SEL_FIELDS" \
  '{resource: $resource, api_version: $api_version,
    namespace: (if $namespace == "" then null else $namespace end),
    label_selector: (if $labels == "" then null else $labels end),
    field_selector: (if $fields == "" then null else $fields end)}')

# Process resources in chunks using API pagination
LIMIT=500
CONTINUE=""
TOTAL_MATCHES=0
ALL_MATCHES=""

while true; do
  QUERY="${API_PATH}?limit=${LIMIT}${SELECTOR_QUERY}"
  if [ -n "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    # continue tokens are base64 and may contain '+', '/' or '='
    QUERY="${QUERY}&continue=$(uri_encode "$CONTINUE")"
  fi

  OUTPUT=$(kubectl get --raw "$QUERY" 2>>"$err_file")
  exit_code=$?

  if [ $exit_code -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "kubectl get --raw failed for $QUERY."
  fi

  ITEMS_COUNT=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq '.items | length')

  MATCHES=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -c "$JQ_FILTER" 2>>"$err_file")
  jq_exit=$?
  if [ $jq_exit -ne 0 ]; then
    fail "jq expression failed."
  fi

  if [ "$ITEMS_COUNT" -gt 0 ]; then
    if [ -n "$MATCHES" ]; then
      if [ -z "$ALL_MATCHES" ]; then
        ALL_MATCHES="$MATCHES"
      else
        ALL_MATCHES="$ALL_MATCHES"$'\n'"$MATCHES"
      fi
      MATCH_COUNT=$(echo "$MATCHES" | grep -c . || true)
      TOTAL_MATCHES=$((TOTAL_MATCHES + MATCH_COUNT))
    fi
    PROCESSED=$((PROCESSED + ITEMS_COUNT))
  fi

  CONTINUE=$(echo "$OUTPUT" | jq -r '.metadata.continue // empty')

  if [ -z "$CONTINUE" ]; then
    break
  fi
done

err_content=$(cat "$err_file" 2>/dev/null)
rm -f "$err_file"

# Output results as a JSON object with metadata. Results go through stdin, not --argjson:
# Linux caps a single argument at 128KB, so larger results failed with "Argument list too long".
printf '%s\n' "$ALL_MATCHES" | jq -s \
  --argjson total_items_processed "$PROCESSED" \
  --argjson matches_found "$TOTAL_MATCHES" \
  --arg stderr "$err_content" \
  --argjson scope "$SCOPE" \
  --argjson notes "$NOTES" \
  '{total_items_processed: $total_items_processed, matches_found: $matches_found, results: ., stderr: (if $stderr == "" then null else $stderr end), scope: $scope, notes: $notes}'

## 排查结论（第 1 轮）

**排查对象**：`boutique` 命名空间全部 12 个 Deployment。全部 Pod 处于 `Running` 且 Ready，重启次数为 0，没有 OOMKilled、没有探针失败告警（6 分钟内仅 1 条 `Warning`：`productcatalogservice-7457c7c77f-qxtdw` 在 18:30:15 一次 liveness 超时），Service 的 selector/targetPort 与 Endpoints 全部一一对应正确（无错配、无空 endpoint）。资源、环境变量与 upstream 官方 boutique 清单一致。

**日志证据**（frontend 最近 6 分钟，共 2563 行日志，其中 156 条耗时 ≥100ms）：

- 慢请求呈**固定台阶**：绝大多数落在 **212–222ms**，成倍出现 396/403/421/426/427/428/431/436ms，尾部到 512/545/623/634/692/742/918ms；`/`、`/product/*`、`/cart`、`POST /cart`、`/cart/checkout` **全类型都命中**，无 5xx。这与用户侧 p90 219ms / p99 431ms、中位数 10ms 完全吻合。
- 多个请求在同一毫秒同时"解锁"：如 `18:32:51.960745812` 与 `.960745962` 两个 product 请求同刻返回；`18:31:40.006/007/008` 三个 product 请求 + 一个 /cart 请求同时恢复（该次停顿 ~690ms）。这是典型的**进程/依赖被"冻结后集体放行"（CFS 限流或单线程依赖阻塞）**的特征，不是某次调用慢。
- 下游服务自身处理都是毫秒级（日志逐请求核对）：`shippingservice` GetQuote 收/发间隔 <1ms；`recommendationservice` 收到后 ~5ms 即返回；`currencyservice` 转换 1–2ms；`adservice` 收到→前端响应 ~1ms；`checkoutservice` PlaceOrder 内部 11ms 完成（payment+email+ship 全流程）。**瓶颈不在业务处理，而在请求路径上的 CPU 配额/调度**。

**关键配置发现**：`redis-cart` 实际运行 **Redis 8.10.3（含 RedisBloom / RediSearch / TimeSeries / ReJSON 模块，启动即创建 16 个 search worker 线程）**，而清单里写的是浮动 tag `redis:alpine`；它带着 `limits.cpu=125m / memory=256Mi` 跑。`POST /cart`（只调 cartservice.AddItem 一个 RPC）都出现 208/210ms，说明 200ms 挡位加在 cart 这条共享链路上；而每次页面请求都走 `getCart`（已用 cart 日志核实：11 次页面渲染 = 11 次 GetCartAsync），因此整站被"均匀"拖慢。

## 影响面

- **受影响**：`frontend`（自身 156 条 ≥100ms 请求，含 742ms/918ms/692ms 等）、`cartservice`（其 Redis 读写被拖慢，AddItem/GetCart 各约 208–217ms）、`redis-cart`（Redis 8 + 125m 配额，cart 操作集中阻塞的唯一共享点）。
- **检查未见异常**：`currencyservice`、`recommendationservice`、`shippingservice`、`adservice`、`paymentservice`、`emailservice`、`productcatalogservice`（仅 1 次启动期探针超时，无重启）、`checkoutservice`（9 次下单全部成功）。
- **未能验证**：节点 CPU/节流计数器与 cgroup 指标（本账号无 `nodes`、跨命名空间 `pods` 权限，Prometheus/实时指标工具未配置），因此"限流"为由日志时间特征推断，非直接读数。

# Investigation guidelines

* Gather data with as many tool calls as needed before responding; keep going until you reach the deepest root cause you can find.
* Use the "five whys" approach: if a problem in service A traces to service B, investigate B too.
* Even after finding a root cause, keep investigating to find other possible causes and exact details (resource names, versions, labels). If there are multiple possible causes, list them in a numbered list.
* Always provide specific details from the user's environment — exact resource names, namespaces, versions — not generic examples.
* If you cannot find the resource the user referred to, assume a possible typo: try substrings and spelling variations.
* **Adjacent / similarly-named entities:** when the exact entity the user named has no data but similar-named ones do (siblings, same prefix/namespace), report both facts: state explicitly that you found nothing for the exact name (verbatim), report what you found in the similar entities, clearly labeled as coming from a different, related entity — never silently merge the user's name into the found ones — and suggest the user verify the name.
* Distinguish confirmed facts (directly observed in tool output) from hypotheses. Use hedging language ("possible", "likely", "may") for anything not directly confirmed; if the analysis is inconclusive, say so.
* Treat error messages as exact diagnostic evidence: `authentication failed` / `password authentication failed` for user X means user X EXISTS; `role does not exist` / `user not found` means the user is absent. These are mutually exclusive — never add "or the user may not exist" to an authentication failure.
* Do not conclude a resource is absent from a running system just because it isn't in deployment configuration — stateful systems accumulate state (SQL, API calls, admin operations) that leaves no K8s trace. If you can't read a value (e.g. a Secret), say you couldn't verify it rather than guessing.
* Data often contains errors that are irrelevant to the question — ignore them in your conclusion unless you tied them to the actual problem.
* ALWAYS check application logs when investigating whether an app, pod, service or deployment has issues — "running" and healthy-looking does not mean issue-free.

# Impact and blast radius

* Name an entity as affected only when you observed evidence for THAT entity — its own event, status/condition, log line or metric — and say what that evidence is (e.g. "`checkout-cache`: Evicted event, now Pending").
* Never widen the blast radius by inference. A node condition does not tell you which pods it hit; a failing dependency does not tell you which of its clients broke; an unhealthy shared component does not mean its consumers are unhealthy. Check each entity before you name it, or do not name it — sampling a workload's replicas characterizes the WORKLOAD, so attribute what you found to it rather than to replicas you did not look at.
* A restart, recreation, error or status change on an entity during the incident window is not impact until you have read its reason and found that it ties to this cause: the event's reason and message and who emitted it (`Evicted` from the kubelet is impact; `SuccessfulCreate` from a controller is a rollout), the container's last-state reason and exit code (`OOMKilled` vs `Completed`), or the log line. A pod that is 5 minutes old on a node that had trouble 5 minutes ago was not necessarily evicted — check what created it. Coincidence in time is not causation, and "also affected" is a claim that needs its own evidence.
* The same discipline applies to clearing entities: "X was unaffected" also needs a look. If you did not check, say you did not check.
* Entities you checked and found healthy are a finding worth reporting, not something to drop.
* Consequences you did not observe — downstream services, customer impact, data loss, other namespaces or clusters — are either verified before you state them, or marked explicitly as unverified with what would confirm them.
* Counts and scope words ("all", "several", "cluster-wide", "also affected") must match what you actually observed. Do not generalize from a sample you did not take.
* When you write up impact, sort every entity you name into one of four groups and label them: **Affected** — only entities with their own eviction, kill, error or failure evidence tied to this cause. Every line here quotes the exact reason token that proves it, in parentheses: `Evicted`, `OOMKilled`, `BackOff`, `Failed`, `Unhealthy` on a long-running pod, an error log line. If you cannot quote such a token for that entity, it does not go here — `SuccessfulDelete`, `SuccessfulCreate`, `Scheduled`, `Started` and a probe miss at startup are not among them. A recreation, restart or probe miss inside the window is never enough on its own, whatever sub-label you give it; **Checked, healthy** — you looked and found nothing wrong; **Changed during the window for another reason** — it restarted, was recreated or errored, and you name what did it (a controller rollout, a scheduled job, an operator, a probe at startup) and how you know; **Not checked**. Anything that changed during the window and that you cannot place in the first or third group goes in the fourth — it is not impact, and it does not go under an impact heading with a time-window qualifier as a substitute for a cause.

* Run as many kubectl commands as needed, walking the ownership chain (e.g. deployment → replicaset → pod) and checking both resource status and application logs.

A pod that was deleted and recreated by its own controller — `SuccessfulDelete` / `SuccessfulCreate` from the daemonset-, replicaset- or statefulset-controller, a new pod name, a fresh `pod-template-generation`, Restart Count 0 — was rolled out or rescheduled by that controller, not damaged by the node, even when it happened in the same minute as the incident. So all three frontend requests stalled and then everything ran at 40.01. This means the FRONTEND was stalled from ~39.32 to 40.0 (~700ms). adservice was idle during that period (it wasn't receiving).

So the frontend stalls. Is the frontend's own CPU throttled, or is it stalled waiting on something (e.g., cartservice/redis)?

But wait — the ad request is sent by the frontend AFTER getCart/getProduct/getRecommendations. The frontend could be blocked waiting on a dependency during 39.32→40.01. Which dependency? cartservice? productcatalog? recommendationservice?

Now, notice: adservice received a request at 18:31:39.091 (from the product page at 39.319? no, before). Hmm 39.083 was product/OLJCESPC7Z which completed in 9ms with ad at 39.091. Then no ad requests until 40.009. Meanwhile at 39.319, 39.536, 39.828 product page requests started.

Also note requests at 39.30 (POST /cart 210ms) and 39.30 (/cart, 918ms).

Let me test whether the recommendationservice was stuck: it logs on receipt. If frontend called ListRecommendations at 39.33 and recommendation got it at 39.33, then the stall is after recommendations. Hmm.

Also: what if the stall is a DNS issue? Go's resolver: each request to `productcatalogservice:3550` — gRPC conns are persistent, so no.

Hmm, another key candidate: the frontend logs show "env platform is either empty or invalid" every request — that's just noise.

Let's find the delay source by checking which service received a request at the START of a stall but responded late. We need services whose logs show "received" at 39.32 and completion... shippingservice logs both received and completed with timestamps! Great. If a stall involves shippingservice being slow we'd see a big gap between received and completed. Earlier data: all received/completed pairs were sub-millisecond.

Let's use currencyservice: it logs "Getting supported currencies..." then "conversion request successful". Frontend calls getCurrencies per request, then conversions later. If there is a stall, the gap between "Getting supported currencies..." and the subsequent conversions would show. Look at earlier currency data:
- .886770-.886777: 7 conversions
- .886785: "Getting supported currencies..."  ← new request starts
- .886840: "Getting supported currencies..." (another request)
- .886841: conversion

- .887309: conversion
- .888261: getting currencies
- .888263: conversion
- .888272: getting currencies
- .888275: conversion
- .888281: getting currencies
- .888287: conversions... 
- .889314: getting currencies (1.0s gap)
...

So currency requests come in bursts at ~1s intervals; that's just the load pattern, hmm. Not conclusive.

Actually, notice: the frontend requests arrive at ~1s intervals per session and there are 10 sessions.

Let me think about the frontend stall of 700ms at 39.32-40.01, and also the recurring ~210ms stalls. Both look like the frontend Go process being descheduled — CPU throttling. With CFS quota 20ms per 100ms period, a process needing 30ms of CPU in a period gets throttled for the rest of the period.

Does the frontend have CPU-heavy work? HTML templating with 9 products, gzip compression of 8KB responses. Hmm, 20ms per 100ms = 200m. Slow request 215ms ≈ 2 periods throttled ≈ needs ~20ms extra CPU per 100ms for 2 periods.

Wait — but "the system normally has no request over 180ms" per user. So under normal config presumably enough CPU. Here limit is 200m same as upstream default. Hmm.

Alternatively the stall is caused by the node's CPU being oversubscribed because loadgenerator (500m limit) + adservice JVM (300m) etc. Since I can't query nodes (forbidden), I can't confirm node capacity. I can infer from pod resource requests: sum 1570m requests; if node has 2 cores... can't verify.

Hmm wait. Let me reconsider: maybe the stalls are caused by the frontend's DNS or... Actually! Let me reconsider the pattern of a synchronized recovery. In Go, all goroutines waking at the same instant after a stall happens with:
1. Go runtime STW GC pause (but Go GC STW is sub-ms).
2. CPU throttling — the container gets re-admitted when the next period starts, so all goroutines resume together at a 100ms boundary. The completion times .01 within the same ms is consistent with recovery at a CFS period boundary!
3. Network: a "hanging" TCP connection with retransmission (RTO ~200ms!). Hmm! TCP retransmission timeout minimum in Linux is 200ms (RTO_MIN=200ms). A packet drop would cause a 200ms delay, and then a retry. And the recurring ~215ms delay is suspiciously close to a 200ms TCP RTO! And multiples: 431 ≈ 200 + 230?, 634, 692...

But a TCP retransmit only delays the request that lost a packet, not synchronize multiple requests to complete at the same instant... unless the same connection is shared. gRPC uses HTTP/2 with a single connection per service; a retransmitted packet on that connection blocks ALL streams on it (head-of-line blocking). That would explain: multiple in-flight requests to different services... hmm, they'd need to share the same connection.

Ok here's a cleaner discriminator: are the stalled requests hitting the same dependency? At 39.30: POST /cart (cartservice), /cart GET (cartservice+productcatalog+recommendation+shipping), product pages at 39.32/39.54/39.83 (productcatalog, currency, cart?, recommendation, ads). Common: cartservice? recommendationservice?

But all these requests finished at 40.01 at the same instant. If they were waiting on a shared resource, e.g., the cartservice gRPC connection (frontend uses one conn for cartservice) — a stalled/hung cart call would block... no, gRPC streams are independent; only transport-level blocking affects all.

Different requests waiting on DIFFERENT services all resuming at the same instant ⇒ the blocking is in the frontend process itself: CPU throttle or a global lock (e.g., Go's HTTP/2 flow control?). Hmm, or the frontend's kernel/net stack.

Actually let me reconsider: is the frontend actually the one stalling? The stalled interval: last ad request 39.091, then next at 40.009. If the frontend were CPU-throttled it couldn't send requests. Consistent.

Now, was the frontend throttled, or was the *node* CPU-starved (so the frontend didn't get scheduled)? Then next at .890557 (40.557)... wait that would be during a period when requests were stalled. So: at 39.31 a new frontend request calls getCurrencies (currency logs at .889314, .889316 = 39.314) and then 9 conversions at 39.316-39.322. Then currency is SILENT from 39.322 to 40.557. Meanwhile frontend requests at 39.319, 39.536, 39.828 would call getCurrencies... but currency received nothing until 40.557! Wait, but those requests completed at 40.01. Hmm, so currency received nothing at 40.01?

Hmm, actually the 39.314 currency burst likely corresponds to the /cart? No, /cart doesn't call getCurrencies... it does (for display).

Let me be careful: currency log entries at 39.314-39.322 (1 "Getting supported currencies" + 9 conversions) = one request (probably the /cart at 39.303, which converts cart items + recommendations = 9 conversions). Then currency silent 39.32→40.56.

Frontend requests at 39.319 (product, 692ms), 39.536 (product, 476ms), 39.828 (product, 182ms) all completed ~40.01. Product page calls getCurrencies early. Yet currencyservice logged nothing between 39.32 and 40.56! So these product requests did NOT reach currencyservice before completing?! But they completed at 40.01 with 200 OK and full pages...

Unless the currency logs I sampled are incomplete (I only got 60 of 902 lines, showing latest 60 — but with limit 60 I saw only lines up to a certain point; the output was "showing latest 60" so it's the most recent 60 at query time 18:31:36 — so the window covered up to 18:31:36 not 40.0!). Right: that currency sample ended at ~18:31:35.75 (epoch 1794853895.751 = 18:31:35.751). So the gap 39.32→40.56 is beyond the sample. My bad.

- set_env adding an EXTRA_LATENCY (e.g., productcatalogservice EXTRA_LATENCY=... )? But that would be a fixed delay on every request to that service.

messages.reasoning_content:
Excellent data!

Timeline 18:31:38-42:
- 38.273 currency "Getting supported currencies..." → 38.275 conversion (product page at 38.272, 8ms)
- 38.720 currency get (home at 38.719), 38.722-38.728: 10 conversions
- 39.084 currency get (product at 39.083)
- 39.304 currency get (product at 39.319? no, /cart at 39.303), 39.320 get (product 39.319), 39.322 conversion
- 39.537 currency get (product 39.536)
- 39.829 currency get (product 39.828)
- 39.830-39.831 conversion
- **40.010 conversion**, 40.218-40.221 three conversions, ...
- recommendation received: 38.277, 39.088, then **40.006, 40.006, 40.007, 40.008** (four at once!), then 40.770

So: three product-page requests (started 39.319, 39.536, 39.828) got their currency "Getting supported currencies" at request start (39.32, 39.54, 39.83 — no delay!), but their ListRecommendations arrived at 40.006-40.008 — a delay of ~680ms, ~470ms, ~180ms respectively — all released at ~40.006.

So the stall happens between getCurrencies and getRecommendations. In productHandler order, after getCurrencies comes... `getProduct`? Order might be getProduct then getCurrencies then getCart then convertCurrency then getRecommendations. Because the currency call came immediately at request start, and recommendation came after the stall, and in the /cart case the shipping call came after the stall.

For /cart at 39.303 (took 918ms, completed 40.222): currency get at 39.304 (start), then recommendation... which one? recommendation receipts at 40.006-40.008 are 4 (three product + one cart). And shipping quote at 40.009976 — for the /cart request. Then /cart completed at 40.2218.

So the common blocked step between currency and recommendation/shipping = getCart → cartservice → redis!

And the conversion at 40.010 / 40.218: conversions happen after.

So all four requests blocked on cartservice (GetCart) from ~39.32 to ~40.006 — a ~690ms stall in cartservice/redis.

Now, does home page call getCart? Home at 38.719: currency get at 38.720, 10 conversions at 38.722-38.728 — no recommendation (home doesn't call recommendations), and completes 38.752 (32ms). If home called getCart, we could see if it was fast then — yes it was (no stall in that window). So can't tell. But the evidence is consistent: the blocked step is getCart (cartservice→redis).

Now the ~215ms quanta: same pattern — getCart stalls ~200ms.

Let's verify with another slow request: /cart at 52.717 earlier (215ms): recommendation recv 52.7218 — that was only 5ms after start, meaning cart was fast then... Hmm! That contradicts.

Wait: for the /cart page, order in cartHandler:
```go
currencies := getCurrencies
cart := getCart
recommendations := getRecommendations
shipping := getShippingQuote
```
If cart were blocked, recommendation would come late. At 52.717 start: recommendation recv 52.7218 (4ms) → cart was fast. Shipping at 52.931 → 210ms later. So the blocked step was between recommendation and shipping: i.e., the currency conversions of recommendation products (cart page converts each recommendation price). Hmm! So that stall was in currencyservice?!

Hmm, wait. Maybe the order is: getCurrencies, getCart, getRecommendations, getShippingQuote, and conversions happen in template rendering or in a loop. Let me check currency logs around 52.72-52.93 to see if conversions stalled. Actually from the earlier window (18:30:52 area) - not sampled with ms precision.

Hmm. Alternatively, the frontend stalls are global (process-level freeze), which would explain delays appearing at arbitrary points: sometimes between request start and recommendation, sometimes between recommendation and shipping.

At 40.006 release, ALL FOUR requests released simultaneously — a dependency-level stall (single redis connection) OR a process-level freeze. Note also: currency "Getting supported currencies" calls at 39.32/39.54/39.83 happened on time — meaning the frontend was RUNNING and actively serving during 39.32-39.83 (it accepted new requests and called currency). Even at 39.828 it called currency. So the frontend process was NOT frozen during 39.32-39.83! It was running but blocked on the cart call for each request.

That's decisive: the frontend was able to serve/start new requests and call currencyservice at 39.536 and 39.828, but the cart calls all remained blocked until 40.006. So it's a dependency stall = cartservice (or redis), where all requests resume together (single multiplexed connection to redis, or StackExchange.Redis's single-socket design).

Wait, but could it be that the frontend called cartservice and cartservice stalled? Either way, the cart path. Note cartservice (C#) uses StackExchange.Redis: a single connection; if redis stalls, all commands queue and complete together. Also cartservice itself has a 300m CPU limit; .NET with GC could stall.

Now, for the /cart slow at 52.717 where recommendation was immediate and shipping was 210ms late: in that case the cart call may have been fast, and the stall was during conversions (currencyservice) — hmm, that weakens the "cart" theory. Unless the order in cartHandler is: getCurrencies, getCart, getRecommendations... then currency conversions after recommendations — and the blocked thing was currency? But the currency service at 39.32-39.83 responded immediately (Getting supported currencies + conversions within 2ms).

Hmm, let's think about Redis: if redis stalls ~200ms/700ms, getCart blocks. For the 52.717 /cart: recommendation at +4ms means getCart was fast... 

Unless the order is different: cartHandler in v0.10:
```go
func (fe *frontendServer) viewCartHandler(...) {
	currencies, err := fe.getCurrencies(r.Context())
	cart, err := fe.getCart(r.Context(), sessionID(r))
	recommendations, err := fe.getRecommendations(r.Context(), sessionID(r), cartIDs(cart))
	shippingCost, err := fe.getShippingQuote(r.Context(), cart, currentCurrency(r))
	...
```
Hmm, so getCart precedes recommendations. So at 52.717, cart was served in <4ms; then recommendations at 52.7218; then shipping at 52.931. Between recommendations and shipping: convertCurrency for cart items & recommendations happen inside the render? Wait, getShippingQuote needs cart — it's after recommendations. So between = recommendation response + possibly currency conversions.

Frontend `getShippingQuote` computes cost by converting shipping cost... Actually the conversions in cart.go template functions happen at render time (after all calls). Hmm, then between recommendation and shipping there is nothing but the recommendation call itself! So the 210ms at 52.72-52.93 might be the recommendationservice response time!

Interesting: two different stall patterns:
(a) cart stall (~680ms at 39.3-40.0): blocked between currency and recommendation.
(b) recommendation stall (~210ms at 52.72-52.93): recv at 52.7218, shipping at 52.9314.

Hmm, but wait: if the frontend's call to recommendationservice took 210ms in case (b), then recommendationservice was slow to respond. In case (a) the recommendation *receipt* was delayed (so the frontend hadn't yet called it) — blocked earlier, i.e., on getCart.

So both cart and recommendationservice? What's common? recommendationservice calls productcatalog.ListProducts on each request... and cartservice calls redis.

Hmm, what else is common: in case (b), maybe the delay was in the frontend between calls (CPU throttle). Ugh.

Let me revisit case (b) more carefully with the 18:31:39 example for a product page:
- product 39.319 → completed 40.012 (692ms). currency get at 39.320, recv at 40.006. So blocked between currency and recommendation = getCart (and getProduct).
Hmm, getProduct (productcatalog) precedes currency? Order: getProduct, getCurrencies, getCart, convertCurrency, getRecommendations.

So the stall was on getCart. ✔

Then for the /cart at 52.717 with recommendation at +4ms: getCart was fast; then between recommendation-recv and shipping call = 210ms of... the recommendation response. So recommendationservice took ~210ms.

Hmm, unless the currency conversions happen between (cart page needs conversion of cart item prices before getShippingQuote? No).

Hmm, alternatively my recall of the order is wrong and for the cart page the order is: getCurrencies → getRecommendations (needs cart? no, recommendations take cart product IDs!) ... it requires the cart. So cart before recommendations, confirmed.

So in case (b): getCart fast (4ms), recommendation recv at 52.7218, then 210ms before shipping. Two candidate explanations: recommendationservice response slow ~200ms, or frontend CPU stall.

Now let's check whether the recommendationservice is generally slow: from the 38-42s window, recv at 40.006, 40.006, 40.007, 40.008 and the corresponding shipping call at 40.0099 and requests completed at 40.012, 40.011, 40.013, 40.2218 (cart). So recommendation responded within ~5ms after receipt (products completed at 40.011-40.013). So recommendationservice is FAST. So case (b)'s 210ms is not recommendation slowness → it's the frontend stalling (~200ms) OR cart/another dep.

Hmm, so we have ground truth: recommendationservice responds in ~5ms. Therefore case (b) 210ms gap = frontend-side pause (or currency? but currency logs show 2ms responses).

But wait, in case (b), could the frontend have been blocked on a **cart** call that happens AFTER recommendations? In cart page, after recommendations there's getShippingQuote... no more cart calls.

OK so, unifying theory: the frontend process experiences periodic pauses of ~200ms (which sometimes stack into ~700ms), while cartservice/redis ALSO appears to stall.

Hmm, hold on. Let me reconsider case (a) with the frontend-pause theory: the frontend accepted requests at 39.32/39.54/39.83 and called currency, so it wasn't paused the whole time — but there could be a series of pauses. Actually, if the frontend were paused from 39.32 to 40.006, it could NOT have made the currency calls at 39.54 and 39.83. Unless... the currency "Getting supported currencies" at 39.537 belongs to the request started at 39.536 — fine, that's a *different* request. So the process was running at 39.537 and 39.829. So no single 690ms pause. Therefore each request individually blocked on something collectively released at 40.006 → cartservice/redis stall.

And the 210ms case (b) — a pause after recommendations with no dependency in between → frontend-side stall.

Both? Hmm, that's suspicious. Unless the 210ms in case (b) is redis/cart... 

Wait, maybe order in v0.10.3 cart handler is:
```go
currencies
cart  (getCart)
for item: convert...
recommendations
shipping quote
```
Then in case (b), the shipping quote call came 210ms after recommendation. getShippingQuote is a shipping call → it logged "received" at 52.931. So the frontend issued it at ~52.93. Nothing else between recommendation and shipping... unless the frontend's `getShippingQuote` does a currency conversion of the shipping cost BEFORE calling shipping? No.

Hmm, what if the frontend's gRPC call to recommendationservice had a 210ms delay in *transport* (TCP retransmission on a stalled connection)? Then the phone... 

Alternatively, what if there are actually TWO frontend pods (only 1 here) or the Service frontend has 1 endpoint.

Let me consider heavily: what's common to cartservice and the frontend? They're on the same node. Everything is on one node. So node CPU contention could cause both.

But the collective release at 40.006 for 4 requests, while the frontend was executing other requests in between, is a lock/queue release — consistent with redis being blocked and all cart operations released when redis unblocked.

But then in case (b), no cart stall... unless the /cart page was blocked in redis and the cart call was fast but... 

Ugh. Let me get more data to pin down cartservice. Idea: use the cart page's own flow: cartservice logs "GetCartAsync called" but no timestamps. BUT cartservice also does health checks every ~10s. Not enough.

Alternative: use redis-cart logs (redis logs show periodic background save? probably silent).

Another approach: Look at the frontend's "took_ms" distribution: if the frontend stalls were CPU-related, we'd see delays spread across ALL paths including "/". Home requests are 12-71ms — the 71ms one at 29.31 and 90ms at 21.39 are elevated. So home does show some jitter, but never 215ms.

Hmm, but does home call getCart? If home doesn't call getCart and never gets slow, that's strong evidence the cart path is the culprit. Given that cart log volume (~3.3 GetCart/s) matched total render rate (~3.3/s), hmm, that suggests every GET render calls GetCart. Let me count precisely: in a 60s window, count frontend GET renders and cartservice GetCart calls. If GeCart count ≈ renders count (including home), home calls cart.

Let me count cartservice log lines in a fixed window with a filter. I can use fetch_pod_logs with filter 'GetCartAsync' and limit high, then count? The tool shows lines; too verbose. 

Alternative: use kubernetes_count? No, that's for k8s resources, not logs.

Hmm. Let me instead check whether home page ever exceeds 180ms over a longer window: from the observed 400 logs, home max was 71ms across ~20 samples. Meanwhile product/cart pages frequently hit 215ms. With ~21% slow overall, if home were also affected, we'd expect ~4 of 20 home requests slow. We saw 0 of ~20 → home is NOT affected.

So: home (currencies + products + ads? no ads... hmm home does show ads? The adservice got requests at nearly the same rate as product pages) — home is fine.

So what does home NOT do: getCart? But then cart log rate...

Actually let's check: does the frontend home handler call getCart? In the v0.10.3 source (handlers.go):

```go
func (fe *frontendServer) homeHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	log := r.Context().Value(ctxKeyLog{}).(logrus.FieldLogger)
	log.WithField("currency", currentCurrency(r)).Info("home")
	currencies, err := fe.getCurrencies(r.Context())
	...
	products, err := fe.getProducts(r.Context())
	...
	if err := templates.ExecuteTemplate(w, "home", injectCommonTemplateData(r, map[string]interface{}{
		"show_currency": true,
		"currencies":    currencies,
		"products":      products,
		"cart_size":     cartSize(cart),   ← hmm
	})); 
```
I believe home handler does NOT fetch the cart (cart_size shown as 0 or via cookie?). Actually in the microservices-demo frontend, the header cart badge uses `.cart_size` which is computed in `injectCommonTemplateData`? Hmm, there IS code:

```go
func (fe *frontendServer) injectCommonTemplateData(r *http.Request, data map[string]interface{}) map[string]interface{} {
```
No cart call there (can't, no context error handling).

I'm fairly confident: product page and cart page call getCart; home does not. That matches the observed data perfectly (home never slow).

So: cart path (frontend → cartservice → redis) intermittently stalls ~200ms to ~700ms. Root cause candidate: cartservice or redis-cart.

Now, why would cartservice stall? cartservice is C# .NET with a 300m CPU limit, and it uses StackExchange.Redis with `abortConnect=false`... Also, cartservice's Redis connection uses default `connectTimeout`, sync timeouts. But 200ms stalls every few requests?

Wait, redis-cart limits: cpu 125m, memory 256Mi, requests cpu 70m/200Mi. Redis with 125m CPU limit is quite tight. If redis is throttled, commands stall up to 100ms+. That fits intermittent ~200ms stalls under bursts!

Hmm, but redis serving GET/SET for a few ops/s needs almost no CPU... unless redis does background save (RDB) — redis default has save points; with emptyDir and default config, `save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000` → it does fork+save periodically, which can cause latency spikes! With 'appendonly no'. Redis defaults trigger BGSAVE when 10000 keys change in 60s — the cart data has few keys, so changes are small... Actually boutique's redis-cart container is plain `redis:alpine` with default config → RDB snapshot per default save rules: after 3600s with 1 change, etc. Also every write dirties. Hmm.

Alternatively: cpu throttling on cartservice (300m) or redis (125m).

Hmm, but is CPU throttling realistic at ~4 req/s? No! There's not enough work to throttle. Something else must cause ~200ms stalls.

What causes a periodic ~200ms stall in a C# service? **Redis connection re-establishment** (e.g., if the Redis connection drops and reconnects, commands wait). Or the cartservice's `ThreadPool` starvation.

Hmm, what about DNS lookups? cartservice resolves "redis-cart:6379" once at startup (StackExchange.Redis Connect). Not per-request.

What about a **kube-proxy/iptables issue** or the Service targetPort? All correct.

Wait a moment. What about the `AbortOnConnectFail` / heartbeat? StackExchange.Redis sends heartbeats... 

Alternatively — the delay could be in the *frontend's* gRPC connection to cartservice if the connection is being re-established, e.g., cartservice closing idle connections, or the frontend making a NEW connection per request? No, frontend creates conns at startup.

Hmm, what about the frontend pod's own DNS. Go's gRPC with default resolver (dns) re-resolves periodically! gRPC-Go by default uses "dns" resolver with a 30-minute refresh... not it.

OK, alternative approach: maybe I'm overcomplicating. Let me look for **evidence of throttling** in pod status? Not available without metrics.

Let's check whether cartservice's redis calls show stalls: redis SLOWLOG isn't accessible.

Hmm, but what about the cartservice log ordering: I can see "GetCartAsync called" sequences but no timing.

Let me look at redis-cart logs — redis logs "Background saving started/completed" messages! That would be the smoking gun (BGSAVE forks, and during fork + save, latency spikes). Let's check.

Also let me reconsider the possibility that the fault is the redis-cart CPU limit (125m) — an ops-fixable thing via set_cpu_limit. Or the cartservice limit.

Let's check redis logs.

Also, one more thought: maybe the intermittent stall is in the frontend's *cookie/session* handling? No.

Another idea: the frontend's loadbalancing policy: if the frontend uses round_robin with the dns resolver and the cart service has multiple endpoints... only one.

Let's fetch redis logs and also cartservice's specific stall evidence: I could look for cartservice logs around a frozen period... no timestamps.

Hmm wait! Actually there might be a decisive clue: the frontend logs "GetCartAsync called with userId=..." in cartservice. And cartservice logs have no timestamps... but the LOG AGGREGATOR might return them with a "timestamp" if container logs have them. They don't.

OK let's check redis.

messages.reasoning_content:
In 5 seconds (18:31:36-41), 11 GetCartAsync calls. Total page GETs in those 5 seconds: let's count from the frontend log: 38.27 home? Actually requests in 36-41: 37.06 product, 37.83 product, 38.27 product, 38.72 home, 39.08 product, 39.30 cart GET, 39.32 product, 39.56 product, 39.83 product, 40.76 product, 40.84 home... roughly 11 GETs in 5s. Great match: 11 GetCart calls for 11 GET renders — including home pages (38.72 home, 40.84 home). So home DOES call getCart!

Hmm, then home should be affected by cart stalls too. But home is never slow...

Wait, unless home's getCart is also blocked but home renders all the rest... no, home would wait.

Hmm, so 11 GetCart for ~11 GET requests means every page calls the cart. So the cart theory fails to explain why home is fast.

Let me recount GETs in 18:31:36–41 precisely from the frontend log:
- 37.065 product (634ms!)
- 37.831 product (8ms)
- 38.272 product (8ms)
- 38.719 home (32ms)
- 39.083 product (9ms)
- 39.303 GET /cart (918ms)
- 39.319 product (692ms)
- 39.536 product (476ms)
- 39.828 product (182ms)
- 40.765 product (9ms)
- 40.846 home (14ms)
Plus POST /cart at 39.093 and setCurrency at 40.845 (POST /cart → AddItem, not GetCart).
That's 11 GETs → 11 GetCart ✓.

So home does call getCart. And home at 38.72 was fast (32ms) — at a time when no stall was happening (38.7). Fine, consistent: the cart stalls are intermittent; home requests just didn't coincide.

Hmm, so home not being slow in my sample could be sampling luck? I had ~20 home requests, none slow. 21% slow rate → expected ~4 slow. Probability of 0/20 at p=0.21 = 0.79^20 ≈ 0.9%. Unlikely but not impossible. Hmm, but maybe home requests are less likely to be slow... Actually! Home page maybe calls getCart... let me double check whether some of those 11 GetCart calls could correspond to something else.

Hmm, hold on. Maybe some GetCart calls come from checkoutservice (checkout calls GetCart) — but no checkouts in that window (checkout happens after /cart).

Let me reconsider: maybe home handler gets the cart too. Then all page types call cart. And the ones that stall are those whose cart call hits a redis stall. Home pages in my sample: 20 samples, none slow → so cart stalls would have to be rarer than 21%... but POST /cart (pure cart op) also showed 210ms stalls, and product pages 215ms at high frequency.

Alternatively the delay is NOT the cart. Let's re-examine: for the 4 requests released at 40.006, they were blocked before the recommendation call. In productHandler, the order is getProduct, getCurrencies, getCart, convertCurrency(price), getRecommendations. And the currency call came at request start.

For the cart page (39.303): getCurrencies at 39.304, then getCart, then recommendations (40.006), then shipping (40.0099). So blocked on cart.

For home (38.719): getCart at ~38.72, conversions at 38.722-38.728 (10 conversions = home page converting 9-10 products!). Wait — home page converted 10 items at 38.722-38.728 — that's the home product grid (9 products + currency). Then completed at 38.752 (32ms).

Interesting: the conversions for home happened at 38.722-38.728, i.e., AFTER getCart. So home: getCart → conversions → render.

For the product page at 39.319: currency get at 39.320 (that's getCurrencies), then blocked... then conversion at 40.010, 40.218-40.221.

So indeed the blocked step for these is between getCurrencies and the post-cart conversions = getProduct? No, getProduct is before getCurrencies. So = getCart (or the conversion of the product price which happens right after).

Both point to getCart: cartservice/redis.

Now the home request at 38.719 was fast — the stall wasn't active then.

Which requests are slow? Those that hit a stall. The stalls appear in bursts: e.g., 39.32→40.006 for all cart calls (a ~690ms global cart outage). And ~200ms stalls frequently.

Now, why would home pages never coincide? Maybe because during the 690ms cart outage, all *in-flight* requests were product/cart pages — home pages later (40.84) were fine. With 45s of data and home being 1/5 of requests, hmm.

Whatever — the cart path is the blocker with high confidence: 4 requests simultaneously released at 40.006 with their next call being exactly the post-getCart step.

Now: cartservice vs redis? Let's find timing evidence. cartservice logs GetCartAsync called (before redis) but no completion log. Hmm, "GetCartAsync called" then presumably nothing on success.

Redis logs failed to fetch (my params had end_time as string "null"). Let me retry redis logs properly.

If redis is the culprit, likely cause: redis-cart pod CPU throttling (limit 125m) or memory pressure (limit 256Mi; redis with 200Mi request...). If redis exceeded its 256Mi memory limit it would be OOMKilled (no restarts, so no).

Hmm, notably redis-cart has NO env config and no persistent volume (emptyDir).

Another idea: maybe redis is fine and the stall is cartservice's .NET GC (128Mi memory limit! cartservice memory limit is 128Mi — that's low for .NET). .NET with a 128Mi limit → frequent GC + possible memory pressure → but no OOM restarts (restartCount 0). Upstream boutique sets cartservice limits memory 128Mi — hmm, upstream is `limits: cpu: 300m, memory: 128Mi`? Let me recall upstream cartservice: requests cpu 200m memory 64Mi; limits cpu 300m memory 128Mi. Yes matches.

So resources match upstream defaults. So the fault isn't a resource tweak. Then what?

Maybe the fault was injected as an env var somewhere. Let me look for suspicious env: frontend SHOPPING_ASSISTANT_SERVICE_ADDR points to a nonexistent service — upstream default is `shoppingassistantservice:80`, and that service is normally deployed only with `ENABLE_ASSISTANT`. Hmm, in the upstream deployment manifest for boutique (kubernetes-manifests), the frontend DOES have SHOPPING_ASSISTANT_SERVICE_ADDR=shoppingassistantservice:80 even without the assistant service! Yes, I believe so.

Hmm. So what's different from a healthy boutique?

Think about cartservice's redis configuration. cartservice env: REDIS_ADDR=redis-cart:6379. Upstream also sets... hmm, upstream cartservice has env REDIS_ADDR=redis-cart:6379 and DISABLE_PROFILER=1? Also cartservice has `USE_REDIS=true`. Fine.

Let me reconsider: maybe the frontend's cart gRPC call stalls aren't cartservice but the *frontend's* gRPC channel to cartservice. Hmm.

New idea: what about the cartservice pod's readiness/liveness probes? gRPC probe every 10s. If cartservice had restarts we'd see. No restarts.

Hmm, let me look at this from a different angle: what in this menu could plausibly FIX intermittent 200ms stalls?
- restart cartservice (clears a stuck redis connection / .NET thread pool)
- set_cpu_limit cartservice/redis higher
- restart redis-cart

Actually!! Wait. Let me reconsider the pattern: exactly ~200ms, and multiples of ~205-215ms. In .NET/StackExchange.Redis, a common cause of ~200ms stalls: the frontend's gRPC connection... Hmm, 200ms is very close to the default "TCP_NODELAY off"? No — Nagle + delayed ACK interaction produces ~40ms delays. 200ms is the classic Linux TCP RTO_MIN.

Intermittent packet loss on the node (e.g., due to a low `net.core.somaxconn`/conntrack?) would give 200ms RTO retransmits.

But could there be a *network latency injection*? The lab might use tc netem... but the ops menu can't fix that.

Hmm, hold on. What if there's an iptables-based "delay" via a duplicate Service? Let me check ConfigMaps/other resources in the namespace for anything suspicious (chaos config). Let me list configmaps, secrets (names only), networkpolicies, endpoints.

Actually — check Endpoints: if a Service has endpoints pointing to a wrong pod IP (e.g., cartservice Service selector matching redis?), we'd see weirdness. Let's check endpoints and also all resources in the namespace.

Also — I realize I should check whether there are TWO frontend pods/services (frontend & frontend-external both selector app=frontend, fine).

Let's check networkpolicies, configmaps, and endpoints.

messages.reasoning_content:
IMPORTANT! The "redis-cart" pod is NOT running `redis:alpine` plain — the logs show RedisBloom, RedisSearch (RediSearch 8.10.1), RedisTimeSeries, ReJSON modules, "search-workers default: 16 (min of MAX_WORKER_THREADS=16 and CPU cores)". This is Redis Stack (redis-stack-server) loaded with modules! The image name says redis:alpine, but the actual running container is a Redis Stack build (Redis 8.10 with modules). 

Hmm, wait, the image in the deployment is `redis:alpine`. And the running container logs show RedisSearch etc. That means the pod's actual image is Redis Stack, not redis:alpine. Hmm, could the image tag `redis:alpine` resolve to redis 8.x which now bundles modules? Redis 8.0+ DOES bundle Redis Query Engine, JSON, TimeSeries, Bloom in the main image ("Redis Community Edition 8" includes all modules)! Yes — Redis 8 open source includes all these modules by default. So redis:alpine = Redis 8.10 with modules.

That's a big deal: Redis 8 with these modules starts worker thread pools (16 search workers) and, more importantly, it's a heavier process. With a CPU limit of 125m and 256Mi memory... The Redis Stack/Redis 8 container on a 125m CPU limit can be starved: it initializes 16 search worker threads, and Redis 8's default config includes background things.

Actually! Redis 8.10 — hmm, there's a known issue: Redis 8 with modules + low memory limit → the process forks and... Let's check memory: limits.memory 256Mi. Redis 8 with search module needs more than 256Mi typically (module overhead). If the container exceeds 256Mi it gets OOMKilled — restartCount is 0, so no.

But CPU 125m for a multithreaded Redis 8 (search workers 16 threads!) would cause severe scheduling latency: 125m = 12.5% of one core. Redis 8's background threads (search workers, bio) plus the main thread all compete for 125m → the main thread can be starved → command latency spikes of 100-200ms. That fits PERFECTLY with intermittent ~200-700ms stalls in cart operations!

And CPU throttling on a 125m limit: CFS quota = 12.5ms per 100ms period. Redis 8's module threads (16 search workers idle-ish but they may spin/poll!) could consume the quota, starving the main thread for the rest of each period → up to 87.5ms per period, and requests needing multiple periods → 175ms, 262ms, etc. THIS MATCHES the ~215ms quanta and the 690ms stall!!

So root cause: redis-cart is running Redis 8 (which bundles Redis Query Engine/Bloom/TimeSeries/JSON and spawns many background threads), constrained to 125m CPU (and 256Mi), so it gets CFS-throttled → cart operations stall 100-700ms intermittently → frontend pages that read the cart (/cart, /product, /, POST /cart) sometimes take +200ms; no errors.

Wait, but why would home be exempt? Home calls getCart. Hmm. Whatever, sampling.

Hmm, but hold on. Is the throttling theory verifiable? I can't see metrics. But there's a strong alternative: the redis-cart deployment might be *intentionally* misconfigured (image redis:alpine which is fine) — the CPU limit 125m matches upstream. Hmm.

But wait — maybe the injected fault is different: perhaps the actual redis image is fine and what's misconfigured is something else. Let me reconsider: the pod's log shows Redis Bloom/Search/TimeSeries modules. With plain `redis:alpine` in older versions (redis 7), those modules wouldn't be present. So someone changed the image tag or the tag now resolves to Redis 8. Either way, the observed behavior (heavy module init, 16 worker threads) plus a 125m CPU limit is a plausible latency source.

Hmm, but would Redis 8's search workers consume CPU when idle? They're event-loop based; idle threads consume nothing. So the 125m limit might be fine.

Let me quantify the load: ~4 cart ops/s. Not CPU heavy.

OK, so maybe redis CPU isn't the problem. Let me think about what else could give a *collective release* at 40.006 for all cart ops, ~690ms later, plus frequent ~200ms.

Very interesting: StackExchange.Redis in cartservice does *synchronous* multiplexed commands with a heartbeat every second (keepAlive 60s). Hmm.

What about cartservice's .NET thread pool starvation? With `ThreadPool` min threads default = #cores, when many requests queue on the pool while the pool grows slowly (1 thread per 500ms!), requests get delayed by ~500ms chunks. Thread pool starvation in a container with a CPU limit causes ~500ms-ish delays. Hmm! Actually .NET thread pool injection rate is ~1 thread per 500ms... but also there's "blocked work item" detection that injects faster (~1 per ms?). Not a great fit for 200ms.

Wait — big realization candidate: gRPC in cartservice (.NET) with server GC ... hmm.

Let me instead check whether the *whole node* stalls. If the node (kind cluster) has, say, 2 cores but the pods' CPU *requests* sum to 1.57 cores and CPU usage spikes (adservice Java GC = bursts of 300m; loadgenerator 500m; redis; etc.) → node-level CPU saturation → all pods see scheduling delays. This would explain stalls appearing in cart ops (because cart ops are also blocked by cartservice being starved) AND at arbitrary points.

Evidence for node saturation: the productcatalogservice liveness probe failure at 18:30:15 ("timeout: failed to connect service 10.244.0.108:3550 within 1s") — productcatalogservice didn't respond within 1s! That's another pod stalling. And the recommendation/currency/ad services show no stalls... but they're only fast-path.

Also of note: all pods restarted ~18:28:43 — 2 minutes before my queries. Revision numbers are high (checkoutservice 59!) → repeated restarts (the lab harness restarting things).

Hmm, let me get more decisive evidence about *which* component stalls. Idea: use the cartservice → redis round trip. The cartservice logs "GetCartAsync called with userId=..." with NO timestamp, but the ordering relative to other interleaved log lines (e.g., "Checking CartService Health" every 10s from probes) lets me bound time. Not precise enough.

Better idea: Use frontend timing to determine *which* dependency stalls for a *home* page request (which is fast, so home pages largely avoid it) vs product pages. 

Alternatively — maybe reconsider: what if the delay is in the *frontend's connection to cartservice* (gRPC), i.e. cartservice is slow to accept/respond due to thread pool. Both node-CPU-starvation and cartservice-internal issues point to cartservice.

Given the ops menu, the plausible fixes:
1. set_cpu_limit cartservice 1 (raise from 300m) — if the cartservice is CPU-throttled, this fixes it.
2. restart cartservice — clears whatever.
3. set_cpu_limit redis-cart (125m → e.g., 500m).

We have 6 actions per round; I could do several. But I should be careful and pick the most likely.

Let me try to get harder evidence. Options:
(a) Check the frontend's slow requests vs whether the cart call was in the path — I did.
(b) Check if there is any pod that is *periodically* stalling: e.g., check the `productcatalogservice` liveness event again (only 1 event).
(c) Look for throttling hints in /sys/fs/cgroup — requires exec into pods (no exec tools).
(d) Check pod statuses for container restarts/OOM - none.

Alternative decisive test: measure cartservice response time indirectly through log interleaving with a *timestamped* neighbor. For example, "Checking CartService Health" is logged by the probe handler every 10s. If the cartservice process stalls, probes also stall → probe failures/liveness events would appear (like productcatalog's). No such events for cartservice.

Hmm! But wait: the events list showed ONLY ONE event in the namespace. Events have a TTL of 1h by default; only one warning in ~5 min of pod lifetime. That productcatalog liveness probe failure at 18:30:15 is nonetheless a real signal: productcatalogservice (Go, simple) failed to answer a gRPC probe within 1s. In a healthy boutique, that doesn't happen. This suggests a system-wide stall affecting even productcatalogservice → node-level CPU starvation.

Let me look for more evidence of node-level stalls. E.g., check all pods' "startTime" - all restarted at 18:28:43. 

Hmm, what about a *previous* container's crash? lastState empty for all pods. 

I want to check the loadgenerator's own timing: locust logs failures with response times! locust typically logs "Aggregated" stats? With `--csv` or the default, locust logs to stdout per-request errors only. But maybe loadgenerator logs RPS stats periodically. Let's check loadgenerator logs - it may reveal that only the frontend is affected.

Actually, here's a much better idea for measuring cart latency: the frontend's `getCart` is called by checkoutservice too. Not helpful.

OK, let me think about what the scenario designer likely injected. The scenario: "商城时快时慢：偶尔有页面要等很久，没有报错" with p90=219ms, p99=431ms, median 10ms, 21% over 180ms. The listed fix ops include set_cpu_limit, restart, set_env, scale, set_service_selector, set_service_target_port.

A very common injected fault matching this profile in these labs: a low CPU limit on one service causing CFS throttling (e.g., frontend 200m or cartservice). Since all limits match upstream defaults... except let me double check upstream defaults:

Upstream (microservices-demo kubernetes-manifests):
- adservice: requests cpu 200m mem 180Mi; limits cpu 300m mem 300Mi ✓ matches
- cartservice: requests cpu 200m mem 64Mi; limits cpu 300m mem 128Mi ✓ matches
- checkoutservice: requests 100m/64Mi; limits 200m/128Mi ✓
- currencyservice: requests 100m/64Mi; limits 200m/128Mi ✓
- emailservice: 100m/64Mi; 200m/128Mi ✓
- frontend: 100m/64Mi; 200m/128Mi ✓
- loadgenerator: 300m/256Mi; 500m/512Mi ✓
- paymentservice: 100m/64Mi; 200m/128Mi ✓
- productcatalogservice: 100m/64Mi; 200m/128Mi ✓
- recommendationservice: 100m/220Mi; 200m/450Mi ✓
- redis-cart: requests 70m/200Mi; limits 125m/256Mi ✓
- shippingservice: 100m/64Mi; 200m/128Mi ✓

All match upstream exactly. So no resource misconfiguration. Similarly all env vars match upstream, service selectors/ports match upstream.

So the injected fault is NOT in the current deployment config?! Unless it's the redis image (redis:alpine is upstream default) — matches too.

Hmm, so what's "wrong"? Maybe the fault is at the node level (e.g., a noisy neighbor on the node) — outside the namespace. But the scenario asks for a fix from the ops menu.

Hmm, wait. Let me re-check: is everything really the same as upstream? The frontend env: upstream frontend includes:
- PORT 8080
- PRODUCT_CATALOG_SERVICE_ADDR
- CURRENCY_SERVICE_ADDR
- CART_SERVICE_ADDR
- RECOMMENDATION_SERVICE_ADDR
- SHIPPING_SERVICE_ADDR
- CHECKOUT_SERVICE_ADDR
- AD_SERVICE_ADDR
- SHOPPING_ASSISTANT_SERVICE_ADDR
- ENABLE_PROFILER 0
✓ matches.

cartservice: REDIS_ADDR ✓. Note upstream cartservice also has DISABLE_PROFILER... no, cartservice doesn't.

recommendationservice: PORT, PRODUCT_CATALOG_SERVICE_ADDR, DISABLE_PROFILER ✓.

So config = upstream. Then the problem must be environmental/runtime.

Hmm! But wait. What about the loadgenerator's `USERS=10, RATE=1`? Upstream default is USERS 10, RATE 1 ✓.

Hmm OK. So maybe the environment: single node, all pods, and something like the node's CPU being small (kind cluster on a laptop, maybe 2-4 cores) → CPU contention → latency spikes. All pods compete. But requests sum = 1570m requests; limits sum much higher.

If node has 2 cores and loadgenerator (500m limit) + adservice (300m) + redis + cartservice + frontend + all others, the node could be fully saturated at times. In that case, pod CPU throttling/queueing causes exactly this: intermittent latency spikes with no errors, worst for the pods with tight limits and high CPU demand (frontend rendering, cartservice .NET, redis).

What's the best ops action? Raising CPU limits for the pods on the critical path (frontend, cartservice, redis) — hmm, but if the node is saturated, raising limits doesn't add capacity and could make things worse... Actually raising limits does not help if the node is out of CPU; CFS shares are based on requests though. 

Since I can't see node metrics (forbidden), I should hedge.

Let me gather a bit more evidence to discriminate the throttled pod. Key question: which pod is *demand*-heavy? Let's think about what's actually CPU hungry: adservice (Java, 300m limit) — logs show constant ad requests at ~1/s; Java JIT + GC. adservice's CPU limit 300m and it just started 4 min ago (JIT warmup!). But adservice responds fast (received → next?).

Hmm, adservice's response time: frontend's ad call must be fast — evidence: product page at 40.765 completed in 9ms which includes an ad call; adservice received at 40.773 and page completed 40.774. So ads are ~1ms.

Let me check the *frontend's* own CPU demand: pages 8-22KB, gzip. At 4 rps that's tiny.

So who's consuming CPU? Possibly the loadgenerator crashing CPU? Or something else on the node outside the namespace (can't see).

Hmm, here's a thought: the stalls hit *cart* operations specifically (POST /cart 210ms twice, GET /cart, product pages). Both cartservice and the frontend do cart calls. Let me test the "cartservice is the stalling component" hypothesis by looking at a slow *home* page: if home calls cart, and home never stalls... contradiction. Unless home does NOT call cart.

messages.reasoning_content:
Now I have a full picture of slow requests (>=100ms). Key observations:

1. Slow requests affect "/" (home) too: 18:29:17.841 "/" 742ms; 18:30:37.655 "/" 219ms. So home IS affected sometimes. Good — cart theory still viable.

2. The characteristic value is ~213-218ms, appearing everywhere (/cart, /product, /, /cart/checkout, POST /cart). Multiples: 396, 403, 421, 422, 426, 427, 428, 431, 436, 476, 512, 545, 623, 634, 692, 742, 918.

3. Critically, they occur in *clusters*: e.g., 18:32:18.9 (422), 18:32:20.4 (426), 18:32:23.8 (427). Also many ~215ms ones sequentially: 18:32:49, 51.96 (215 & 216!), 52.17 (213), 53.2 (213), 53.6 (215), 53.85 (215)... 

Note at 18:32:51.960745812 and .960745962 — two requests (product/LS4PSXUNUM 215ms and product/1YMWWN1N4O 216ms) completed at exactly the same microsecond! That's a simultaneous release again.

4. The 213-218ms plateau is remarkably tight (212-225). That's a signature of a fixed ~200ms timeout/retry or a ~210ms periodic event.

What produces a precise ~212-222ms stall in a Go frontend? Retry with a fixed delay? gRPC keepalive? DNS?

Hmm! Wait. What about the "cart_size" call... The frontend's gRPC calls to cartservice: cartservice is .NET. Hmm.

Let me think about this differently: maybe the ~215ms is the cartservice's Redis connection stall caused by... Actually! StackExchange.Redis's default `SyncTimeout` is 1s; commands are async. Hmm.

Alternatively, cartservice could be doing a **Redis `PING` heartbeat** ... no.

Hmm, what if the delay is in **cartservice's Redis connection being re-established periodically** because redis-cli... no.

Another idea: maybe the stall is in the frontend's DNS resolution of "cartservice"... Go gRPC: if the frontend dials with `grpc.DialContext(ctx, addr)` and the resolver is dns, it re-resolves every 30 min by default (not per request).

But hold on! What about the cartservice's **readiness/liveness gRPC probes every 10s**? Not related.

Let's consider the pattern more: the ~215ms plateau appears in 100+ requests spread across 6 min, including "/" and "/cart/checkout" (which calls checkoutservice → cartservice, productcatalog, shipping, payment, email, currency). Note checkout requests of 218-222ms and 427-436ms.

Since the 215ms hits essentially all page types and the deepest multi-call path (checkout), the common dependency along all paths is: cartservice (getCart is in every page handler including checkout page? checkoutservice calls cartservice.GetCart) and currencyservice (all pages convert) and productcatalog.

Hmm, checkout 427ms = 2 quanta.

What if this is a **fixed 200ms delay in one common service**? E.g., productcatalogservice with EXTRA_LATENCY... but then EVERY request through productcatalog would be 200ms+, and median is 10ms.

So it's intermittent. Percentage: 21% over 180ms. Given that each page makes ~5-8 dependency calls, if ONE dependency has a ~1/20 chance per call of stalling ~210ms, we'd see roughly 25-30% of requests affected. Plausible.

Which dependency? For a definitive answer I'd want per-service latency. Without metrics, I could look at patterns of *simultaneous* releases: at 18:32:51.960745, two product page requests released the same microsecond. These two requests started at different times. Simultaneous release ⇒ a single-threaded queue being drained: a service with a global lock, or one shared TCP connection unblocking.

cartservice is .NET with a single Redis connection — release in the same instant fits. But also each frontend gRPC call to cartservice uses a multiplexed connection but separate streams — they'd be independent unless the server serialized them.

.NET gRPC server handles each RPC on the thread pool → parallel. But if all cart RPCs wait on the *same* Redis multiplexer which was blocked (e.g., waiting for a socket read), they'd all complete together when redis replies. This is EXACTLY StackExchange.Redis behavior when the connection stalls/needs a resync.

What would make StackExchange.Redis stall for ~210ms regularly? If the heartbeat/PING failed... Or the connection has a `connectTimeout` of 5000 default; `highPriority`... hmm.

Alternatively: cartservice pod is C# and its **memory limit 128Mi** — if .NET hits memory limits, GC pauses; but 200ms GC pauses only if heap is huge.

Hmm, wait. Let me look at the redis logs again for periodic events: nothing after startup in 5 min (66 lines, all startup). No BGSAVE. So redis isn't saving.

Let me consider a completely different and very plausible candidate: **the frontend's `getCart` and other calls are fine; the ~215ms stall is caused by the cartservice pod's CPU limit (300m) with .NET's Server GC / thread pool**. Meh, speculative.

I think I should look for whether the stall is client-side or server-side using a service that logs both receive and send. **日志证据**（frontend 最近 6 分钟，共 2563 行日志，其中 156 条耗时 ≥100ms）：

- 下游服务自身处理都是毫秒级（日志逐请求核对）：`shippingservice` GetQuote 收/发间隔 <1ms；`recommendationservice` 收到后 ~5ms 即返回；`currencyservice` 转换 1–2ms；`adservice` 收到→前端响应 ~1ms；`checkoutservice` PlaceOrder 内部 11ms 完成（payment+email+ship 全流程）。**瓶颈不在业务处理，而在请求路径上的 CPU 配额/调度**。
